title: Python Fundamentals
description: Learn the foundations of Python: syntax, variables, data types, operators, input/output and beginner programs.

topics.title: Introduction to Python
topics.matter: Python is a high-level programming language designed to make programming readable and productive. Its clear syntax allows beginners to focus on solving problems instead of dealing with unnecessary complexity. Python is widely used for automation, web development, data analysis, artificial intelligence and machine learning. In this lesson, learners understand what Python is, where it is used and how to run a first program.
subconcepts: Python is a general-purpose programming language known for readable syntax and a large standard library.
Python is used in automation, web applications, data analysis, AI/ML, testing and many other areas.
The print() function is one of the simplest ways to display information on the screen.
topics.practice: Write a program that displays a short welcome message for a programming course.

topics.title: Python Syntax
topics.matter: Syntax is the set of rules that determines how Python statements must be written. Python uses indentation to organize blocks of code, and it is case-sensitive, so uppercase and lowercase names are different. Comments can be added to explain code without affecting program execution. Understanding syntax early helps learners read error messages and write clean programs.
subconcepts: A statement is an instruction that Python executes, such as an assignment or a function call.
Indentation groups related statements inside structures such as if statements and loops.
Comments begin with # and help explain code to people without being executed by Python.
topics.practice: Write a small program containing one comment and two print statements.
example:
# Display a course message
print("Python practice")

topics.title: Variables
topics.matter: A variable is a name used to store information so a program can use that information later. Python creates a variable when a value is assigned to a name, and it automatically determines the value's data type. Meaningful names make programs easier to understand, while reassignment allows stored information to change during execution.
subconcepts: Use the assignment operator = to store a value under a meaningful name.
Names may contain letters, numbers and underscores, but should not start with a number.
Assigning a new value to an existing variable replaces the previous value.
topics.practice: Create variables for a product name, quantity and price, then display them.

topics.title: Data Types
topics.matter: A data type describes the kind of value stored in a variable. Common beginner types are int for whole numbers, float for decimal numbers, str for text and bool for True or False values. Knowing the type of data helps learners choose suitable operations and avoid unexpected results.
subconcepts: The int type represents whole numbers such as 5, 100 or -3.
The float type represents numbers containing a decimal part.
The str type stores text inside quotation marks.
The bool type stores either True or False.
topics.practice: Create one variable of each basic type and display its type.

topics.title: Type Conversion
topics.matter: Type conversion changes a value from one data type to another when the program requires it. Functions such as int(), float() and str() are commonly used for conversion. This is especially important when working with input because input() returns text, even when the user enters a number.
subconcepts: Converts a suitable value to an integer.
Converts a suitable value to a decimal number.
Converts a value to text so it can be combined with strings.
topics.practice: Take a number stored as text, convert it to an integer and add 10.

topics.title: Operators
topics.matter: Operators are symbols or keywords used to perform operations on values. Arithmetic operators perform calculations, comparison operators compare values, assignment operators update variables, and logical operators combine conditions. Operator precedence determines the order in which an expression is evaluated.
subconcepts: Use +, -, *, /, //, %, and ** for common numerical operations.
Operators such as ==, !=, >, <, >= and <= compare values and produce a Boolean result.
and, or and not combine or modify conditions.
topics.practice: Build a program that calculates the total cost of two products.

topics.title: Input and Output
topics.matter: Programs become interactive when they can receive information from users and display useful results. Python uses input() to read keyboard input and print() to display output. Because input() returns a string, numerical input normally needs conversion before arithmetic operations are performed.
subconcepts: Displays text or values on the screen.
Reads a value entered by the user and returns it as a string.
Output can combine labels and values to make results easier to understand.
topics.practice: Ask the user for a product name and quantity and display a sentence using both values.
example:
city = input("Enter a city: ")
print("Selected:", city)

topics.title: Simple Python Programs
topics.matter: Small programs combine multiple basic concepts to solve a specific problem. Instead of learning syntax in isolation, learners should practice turning a simple requirement into variables, input, calculations and output. These programs provide the foundation for larger applications.
subconcepts: Use dimensions and arithmetic operators to calculate the area of a shape.
Add values and divide by the number of values to find an average.
Use a mathematical formula to convert one measurement into another.
topics.practice: Create a simple program that calculates the area of a rectangle.
example:
a = 70
b = 80
c = 90
avg = (a + b + c) / 3
print("Average:", avg)

topics.title: Calculator Activity
topics.matter: A calculator is a useful first mini-application because it combines input, type conversion, arithmetic operators and output in one program. Learners can begin with two numbers and then extend the program with more operations and validation.
subconcepts: Use operators to calculate addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.
Accept the two values that the calculator should process.
Check for situations such as division by zero before calculating.
topics.practice: Build a two-number calculator with addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.

title: Control Flow and Functions
description: Learn decisions, loops and reusable functions to control how Python programs execute.

topics.title: if, elif and else
topics.matter: Conditional statements allow a program to choose different actions depending on whether a condition is true or false.
subconcepts: Conditions produce True or False results.
elif checks another condition when earlier conditions are false.
A condition can contain another decision when a problem requires multiple levels of checking.
topics.practice: Create a program that categorizes a number as positive, negative or zero.

topics.title: for and while Loops
topics.matter: Loops repeat a block of code so that a task does not have to be written again and again. for is commonly used when iterating over a sequence or known range, while repeats while a condition remains true.
subconcepts: Repeats code for each item in a sequence or range.
Repeats code while its condition remains true.
Generates a sequence of numbers useful for controlled repetition.
topics.practice: Print the first ten natural numbers using a loop.

topics.title: break, continue and pass
topics.matter: Loop-control statements change the normal flow of a loop. break stops a loop, continue skips the current iteration, and pass acts as a placeholder when code is intentionally left empty.
subconcepts: Skips the remaining statements for the current iteration.
Does nothing and is useful as a temporary placeholder.
topics.practice: Print numbers from 1 to 10 but skip 5.

topics.title: Functions
topics.matter: Functions group instructions into a reusable block. They reduce repetition and make programs easier to organize, test and maintain. A function can accept inputs through parameters and can send a result back using return.
subconcepts: Parameters allow a function to receive values from the caller.
return sends a result back to the place where the function was called.
A function can be called multiple times with different inputs.
topics.practice: Create a function that returns the square of a number.

topics.title: Nested Conditions
topics.matter: Nested conditions place one decision inside another. The outer condition is checked first, and only when it is true does Python evaluate the inner condition. This is useful for layered eligibility, validation and access decisions.
subconcepts: Controls whether the inner block is reached.
Each nesting level must use consistent indentation.
topics.practice: Create a program that checks two related eligibility conditions.

topics.title: Function Parameters and Arguments
topics.matter: Parameters are names defined in a function, while arguments are the actual values supplied when the function is called. Parameters make functions reusable because the same logic can work with different data.
subconcepts: Variables listed in a function definition.
Values supplied to a function call.
A parameter can have a default value.
topics.practice: Write a function that accepts a student name and displays a message.

topics.title: Return Values
topics.matter: The return statement sends a result from a function back to the calling code. Returned values can be stored, printed, combined with other expressions or passed into another function.
subconcepts: Ends the function and sends a value back.
A returned value can be stored or reused.
A function without an explicit return normally produces None.
topics.practice: Create a function that returns the total cost from price and quantity.

topics.title: Scope and Local Variables
topics.matter: Scope describes where a variable name can be accessed. Variables created inside a function are normally local to that function, while names defined outside functions belong to the wider module scope. Understanding scope helps prevent unintended changes.
subconcepts: A variable created inside a function is normally available only there.
A name created outside functions has wider module scope.
Scope determines where a name can be used.
topics.practice: Write a function with a local variable and display it from inside the function.

title: Data Structures
description: Work with lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries to organize collections of data.

topics.title: Lists
topics.matter: A list stores multiple values in an ordered and changeable collection. Lists are useful for groups of related data such as products, marks or tasks.
subconcepts: Access an item using its position, starting from index 0.
Adds an item to the end of a list.
Selects a range of items from a list.
topics.practice: Create a list of five subjects and print the third subject.

topics.title: Tuples
topics.matter: A tuple is an ordered collection that cannot be changed after creation. Tuples are useful for fixed groups of related values.
subconcepts: Tuples are usually written with parentheses.
Tuple elements can be accessed using indexes.
Tuple elements cannot be replaced after creation.
topics.practice: Create a tuple containing three course names and display the second one.

topics.title: Sets
topics.matter: A set stores unique values and is useful when duplicates should be removed or membership needs to be checked efficiently.
subconcepts: Sets automatically keep only unique elements.
The in operator checks whether a value exists in a set.
Union and intersection combine or compare sets.
topics.practice: Create two sets of numbers and find their common values.

topics.title: Dictionaries
topics.matter: A dictionary stores information as key-value pairs. It is useful when data needs meaningful labels instead of numeric indexes.
subconcepts: Each dictionary entry connects a key with its corresponding value.
Use a key to retrieve its value.
Assign a new value to an existing key to update information.
topics.practice: Create a dictionary containing a book title, author and price.

topics.title: List Methods
topics.matter: List methods provide ready-made operations for changing and inspecting list data. Common methods include append(), insert(), remove(), pop(), sort() and reverse(). Learning these methods makes collection processing shorter and clearer.
subconcepts: Adds an item to the end.
Adds an item at a chosen position.
Remove an item by value or position.
topics.practice: Create a subject list, add a subject, and remove one subject.

topics.title: List Slicing
topics.matter: Slicing extracts a selected portion of a sequence without changing the original list. The start index is included, the stop index is excluded, and an optional step controls how positions are selected.
subconcepts: Controls the interval between selected items.
topics.practice: Use slicing to display the first three elements and a reversed version of a list.

topics.title: Tuple Packing and Unpacking
topics.matter: Tuple packing groups multiple values into one tuple, while unpacking assigns tuple elements to separate variables. This is useful for fixed groups of data and for functions that return multiple values.
subconcepts: Combines multiple values into a tuple.
Functions can return several values as a tuple.
topics.practice: Create a tuple containing a course and duration, then unpack it.
example:
point = (12, 18)
x, y = point
print(x, y)

topics.title: Dictionary Methods
topics.matter: Dictionary methods make it easier to read, update and inspect key-value data. Important methods include get(), keys(), values(), items(), update() and pop().
subconcepts: Reads a value and can provide a default.
topics.practice: Create a student dictionary and use get() and update().

title: File Handling and Exception Handling
description: Read and write files and handle runtime problems without crashing the application.

topics.title: Reading and Writing Files
topics.matter: File handling allows a Python program to store information outside the running program. Files can be opened in modes such as read, write and append. Using with is recommended because it automatically manages closing the file.
subconcepts: Common modes include r for reading, w for writing and a for appending.
with safely manages a file resource and closes it after use.
read() gets file content while write() stores text.
topics.practice: Create a text file and write three lines into it.
example:
with open("notes.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("Practice Python")

with open("notes.txt", "r") as file:
    content = file.read()
print(content)

topics.title: Exception Handling
topics.matter: Exceptions are runtime problems that interrupt normal execution. Python provides try and except so a program can respond to expected errors and continue safely. finally can be used for cleanup that should happen regardless of success or failure.
subconcepts: Contains code that may raise an exception.
Runs after the try/except process whether an exception occurred or not.
topics.practice: Write a program that safely converts user input into an integer.

topics.title: File Modes and Paths
topics.matter: The open() function uses a path and mode to control file access. Common modes are r for reading, w for writing or replacing content, a for appending, and x for creating a new file.
subconcepts: a adds content to the end.
topics.practice: Append one line to a text file.
example:
with open("log.txt", "a") as file:
    file.write("New entry\n")
print("Entry added")

topics.title: with Statement for Files
topics.matter: The with statement creates a managed context for file operations and automatically closes the file when the block ends. It keeps file-handling code clean and reduces resource-management mistakes.
topics.syntax:
with open(file_path, mode) as file:
    data = file.read()
subconcepts: Manages setup and cleanup for the file.
The file is closed when the with block finishes.
Related file operations stay inside one block.
topics.practice: Read a text file using with and print its contents.
example:
with open("data.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("File content")

with open("data.txt", "r") as file:
    content = file.read()
print(content)

topics.title: File Exceptions
topics.matter: File operations can fail when a path is incorrect or access is unavailable. Handling expected exceptions lets the program display a useful message instead of terminating unexpectedly.
subconcepts: Raised when the requested file does not exist.
Can occur when access is not allowed.
Catch the expected exception for clearer feedback.
topics.practice: Handle a missing-file error with a helpful message.

topics.title: Custom Exceptions
topics.matter: Custom exceptions represent application-specific error conditions. A custom exception normally inherits from Exception and is raised when a program rule is violated. This makes validation errors easier to identify and handle.
subconcepts: Custom errors can be caught with except.
topics.practice: Create a custom exception for an invalid score.

title: Object-Oriented Programming
description: Understand classes, objects, constructors, methods, inheritance and encapsulation.

topics.title: Classes and Objects
topics.matter: Object-oriented programming models software using classes and objects. A class defines a structure and behavior, while an object is an instance created from that class. This approach helps organize larger programs around meaningful entities.
subconcepts: A class is a blueprint that defines attributes and behavior.
An object is an instance of a class.
A method is a function defined inside a class.
topics.practice: Create a Student class with one method that displays a course name.

topics.title: Constructors and self
topics.matter: The __init__ method initializes object data when an object is created. The self parameter refers to the current object and is used to access its attributes and methods.
subconcepts: Runs automatically when an object is created.
Store information belonging to an object.
topics.practice: Create a class with a constructor that stores a person's name and age.

topics.title: Inheritance
topics.matter: Inheritance allows one class to reuse and extend features of another class. It is useful when several classes share common behavior but also need their own specialized behavior.
subconcepts: Inherits features and can add its own behavior.
Inheritance reduces duplication when classes share common functionality.
topics.practice: Create a base Shape class and a Rectangle child class.

topics.title: Instance Attributes and Methods
topics.matter: Instance attributes store data separately for each object, while instance methods define behavior that can use that data. The self parameter refers to the current object.
subconcepts: Data stored for an individual object.
A function inside a class that works with an object.
topics.practice: Create a class with one attribute and one method.

topics.title: Encapsulation
topics.matter: Encapsulation groups related data and behavior inside a class and encourages controlled access to internal state. Python commonly uses naming conventions such as a leading underscore and properties or methods to validate updates.
subconcepts: A leading underscore communicates intended internal use.
Methods can validate values before changing state.
Properties can provide controlled access to attributes.
topics.practice: Design a class that stores an internal score and updates it safely.

topics.title: Polymorphism
topics.matter: Polymorphism allows different classes to provide a common method name while implementing behavior appropriate to each object. Code can then work with different object types through a shared interface.
subconcepts: Different classes can expose the same method name.
Each class can implement the method differently.
Common method calls reduce type-specific branching.
topics.practice: Create two classes with the same method name and different results.

topics.title: Method Overriding
topics.matter: Method overriding occurs when a subclass defines a method with the same name as a parent method. The child implementation is used for child objects, and super() can be used when parent behavior is also needed.
subconcepts: Child classes can use parent behavior.
A child can replace a parent method.
Can access parent behavior when needed.
topics.practice: Create a parent and child class where the child overrides one method.

title: Database Connectivity
description: Connect Python with SQLite, create tables, insert data and perform CRUD operations.

topics.title: SQLite Connection
topics.matter: SQLite is a lightweight relational database that stores data in a local file. Python includes the sqlite3 module, so a separate database server is not required for basic projects. A connection object lets the program execute SQL statements and manage transactions.
subconcepts: Opens a connection to the SQLite database file.
Executes SQL statements and retrieves results.
Saves changes made by INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE.
topics.practice: Create a SQLite database connection and close it correctly.
example:
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect("school.db")
print("Connected")
conn.close()

topics.title: CRUD Operations
topics.matter: CRUD stands for Create, Read, Update and Delete. These operations form the basic workflow for managing records in a database-backed application. Python can execute parameterized SQL statements through sqlite3.
topics.practice: Create an items table and insert three records.
example:
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("CREATE TABLE items(name TEXT)")
cur.execute("INSERT INTO items(name) VALUES (?)", ("Pen",))
conn.commit()

cur.execute("SELECT name FROM items")
print(cur.fetchall())
conn.close()

topics.title: Parameterized Queries
topics.matter: Parameterized queries separate SQL instructions from user-provided values. They improve correctness and help protect applications from SQL injection because values are passed separately from the SQL statement.
subconcepts: Passed as a separate sequence or tuple.
User values are treated as data instead of SQL code.
topics.practice: Write a parameterized query that searches by student name.
example:
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("CREATE TABLE users(user_id INTEGER, name TEXT)")
cur.execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?)", (7, "Ravi"))

cur.execute("SELECT name FROM users WHERE user_id = ?", (7,))
print(cur.fetchone())
conn.close()

topics.title: Transactions and Commit
topics.matter: A transaction groups database changes into a unit of work. commit() saves successful changes, while rollback() can undo uncommitted changes after an error. Transactions help keep related operations consistent.
subconcepts: Related operations can be handled as one unit.
topics.practice: Insert a record and commit it, then test rollback with another change.
example:
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE student(name TEXT)")
conn.execute("INSERT INTO student VALUES (?)", ("Asha",))
conn.commit()

conn.execute("INSERT INTO student VALUES (?)", ("Temp",))
conn.rollback()

print(conn.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM student").fetchone()[0])
conn.close()

topics.title: Database Constraints
topics.matter: Constraints are rules enforced by a database to keep stored data valid. Primary keys identify rows, NOT NULL requires values, UNIQUE prevents duplicates, and foreign keys maintain relationships between tables.
topics.syntax: CREATE TABLE student(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL)
topics.practice: Create a table with primary key and NOT NULL constraints.
example:
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE users(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL)")
conn.execute("INSERT INTO users(email) VALUES (?)", ("a@example.com",))
try:
    conn.execute("INSERT INTO users(email) VALUES (?)", ("a@example.com",))
except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
    print("Duplicate emails are blocked")
conn.close()

topics.title: Parameterized CRUD Workflow
topics.matter: CRUD means Create, Read, Update and Delete. A complete SQLite workflow should use parameterized SQL, commit successful writes and verify records before updating or deleting them.
topics.practice: Build a student-record workflow that performs all four CRUD operations.
example:
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("CREATE TABLE student(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)")
cur.execute("INSERT INTO student(name) VALUES (?)", ("Asha",))
cur.execute("UPDATE student SET name=? WHERE id=?", ("Riya", 1))
cur.execute("SELECT name FROM student WHERE id=?", (1,))
print(cur.fetchone()[0])
cur.execute("DELETE FROM student WHERE id=?", (1,))
print(cur.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM student").fetchone()[0])
conn.close()

title: API Integration, Automation and Reporting
description: Use APIs, automate repetitive work and create simple reports from program data.

topics.title: Working with APIs
topics.matter: An API allows one software system to communicate with another using defined requests and responses. Python can send HTTP requests to public services and process JSON data. Learners should understand endpoints, parameters, status codes and response data before building API-based applications.
subconcepts: An endpoint is a URL provided by an API for a particular resource or operation.
JSON is a common format for exchanging structured data.
HTTP status codes indicate whether a request succeeded or failed.
topics.practice: Call a public test API and print one field from its JSON response.
example:
import json

response_text = '{"name": "Alex", "score": 90}'
data = json.loads(response_text)
print(data["score"])

topics.title: Automation
topics.matter: Automation uses programs to perform repetitive tasks consistently. Python can automate file processing, data transformation, scheduled tasks and other routine workflows. Good automation scripts validate inputs and report errors clearly.
subconcepts: Loops allow the same operation to be applied to many items.
Programs can organize or process files with suitable safeguards.
Automation should verify inputs and expected conditions before making changes.
topics.practice: Process a list of five numbers automatically and print their squares.

topics.title: Reporting
topics.matter: Reporting converts processed information into a format that is easier to understand and share. Python can calculate totals, averages and summaries and then write results to text, CSV or other formats. Clear labels and consistent formatting make reports useful.
subconcepts: Combine raw values into useful totals, counts or averages.
Use clear labels and consistent structure in reports.
Save report content to a suitable file format.
topics.practice: Create a small report showing the count and average of five numbers.
example:
scores = [70, 80, 90]
avg = sum(scores) / len(scores)
print("Average:", avg)

topics.title: JSON Data
topics.matter: JSON is a lightweight text format commonly used for API responses and configuration. Python can convert JSON text into dictionaries and lists with the json module, making structured web data easier to process.
subconcepts: JSON objects commonly become Python dictionaries.
JSON arrays commonly become Python lists.
json.loads() converts JSON text into Python data.
topics.practice: Parse a small JSON string and print one value.
example:
import json

text = '{"name": "Asha"}'
data = json.loads(text)
print(data["name"])

topics.title: HTTP Requests with Python
topics.matter: Python programs can communicate with web services over HTTP. The requests library provides a simple interface for GET and other request methods. Applications should use timeouts and check response status before processing data.
subconcepts: Indicates whether a request succeeded or failed.
topics.practice: Write a GET request with a timeout and display the status code.
example:
import requests

response = requests.get("https://example.com", timeout=10)
print(response.status_code)
topics.run_note: Needs internet and the 'requests' library, so it cannot run inside the Practice Lab. Run it on your own computer.

topics.title: API Error Handling
topics.matter: API calls can fail because of network problems, invalid URLs or server-side errors. Reliable programs catch request exceptions, verify status codes and show useful fallback messages instead of assuming every response is valid.
subconcepts: Base exception for many requests-related failures.
Provides useful behavior when a request fails.
topics.practice: Add exception handling around an HTTP request.
example:
import requests

try:
    response = requests.get("https://example.com", timeout=5)
    response.raise_for_status()
    print("Request successful")
except requests.RequestException:
    print("Request failed")
topics.run_note: Needs internet and the 'requests' library, so it cannot run inside the Practice Lab. Run it on your own computer.

topics.title: CSV Reporting
topics.matter: CSV stores tabular information as rows and columns. Python’s csv module can create reports that are easy to open in spreadsheet applications or process with other programs.
subconcepts: Writes Python sequences as CSV records.
topics.practice: Generate a two-column CSV report containing names and scores.
example: Write and read a CSV report

import csv

with open("report.csv", "w", newline="") as file:
    writer = csv.writer(file)
    writer.writerow(["Name", "Score"])
    writer.writerow(["Asha", 90])

with open("report.csv", "r", newline="") as file:
    for row in csv.reader(file):
        print(row)

topics.title: Scheduled Automation Concepts
topics.matter: Automation combines repeatable Python logic with a trigger such as an operating-system scheduler. Good automation scripts validate inputs, handle errors and produce useful logs or reports so that repeated work is reliable.
subconcepts: An external scheduler determines when a task runs.
Records what an automated task did.
topics.practice: Design a small function that could be scheduled to generate a daily report.
